Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: The vector $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ because its entries sum to $1$ and its $\ell^1$ norm is $1\le C$. Thus the coefficient set is nonempty. It is closed: the sum constraint is the inverse image of the closed singleton $\{1\}$ under a continuous linear map, and the $\ell^1$ bound is the inverse image of the closed interval $(-\infty,C]$ under the continuous function $c\mapsto\sum_i|c_i|$. It is bounded because $\|c\|_1^2=\sum_i c_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}|c_i||c_j|\ge\|c\|_2^2$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. Therefore [F2] makes $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ compact.

The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$.

For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$.

If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking.

derivations.claim: Since $\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)=\lambda_r(H_0)+g$, we have $R=\lambda_r(H_0)-\lambda_1(H_0)+g/2\ge g/2>0$. Reversing the descending-index convention in [F1] gives the same perturbation bound for the ascending eigenvalues used here. Thus if $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, then $\lambda_1(H)\ge c-g/4$ and $\lambda_r(H)\le c+R-g/4$. Since $R-g/4\ge g/4$, every first-$r$ eigenvalue therefore satisfies $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\le R-g/4$, so it lies at least $g/4$ inside the circle centered at $c$.

The same eigenvalue estimate gives $\lambda_{r+1}(H)\ge c+R+g/4$, so all remaining eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\ge R+g/4$ and lie at least $g/4$ outside the circle. By [F2], the spectrum of $H$ is real and $H$ diagonalizes unitarily. For every $z\in\Gamma$, reverse triangle gives $|z-\lambda_j(H)|\ge||z-c|-|\lambda_j(H)-c||\ge g/4$ by steps 1.1–1.2. Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $r$ be an integer with $1\le r<n$. Use Hermitian
adjoints and matrices as in [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], trace as in
[[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]], and the Frobenius norm as in
[[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Write
$$\mathbb H_n:=\{A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}:A=A^*\}$$
for the real vector space of Hermitian matrices, with Frobenius inner product
$$\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB).$$
The **rank-$r$ orthogonal projector domain** is
$$\mathcal P_r:=\{P\in\mathbb H_n:P^2=P,\ \operatorname{tr}P=r\}.$$
An element of $\mathcal P_r$ is an orthogonal projector; its range is the occupied
subspace. The statement that its range has dimension $r$ is justified by
[[lem-hermitian-idempotent-trace-equals-rank]]. A frame $Y\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$
with $Y^*Y=I_r$ represents $P=YY^*$; replacing $Y$ by $YQ$ for a unitary
$Q\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}$ leaves $P$ unchanged.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors.

Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector.

The operator in step 2.1 is independent of all allowed basis choices, lies in $\mathcal P_r$ by [L1], and is exactly the map specified by [F2]. Hence it is the unique rank-$r$ occupied spectral projector.

derivations.claim: The diagonal matrix $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r$ ones is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D_0\preceq I_n$, and has trace $r$. Thus $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$, so the domain is nonempty.

Let $(D_k)$ be a Frobenius-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$. Each real and imaginary matrix entry is Cauchy because $| (D_k-D_\ell)_{ij}|\le\|D_k-D_\ell\|_F$. By [F2] the finitely many coordinates converge, defining a matrix $D$; conjugate symmetry passes to coordinate limits, so $D=D^*$.

For every fixed $x\in\mathbb C^n$, entrywise convergence gives $x^*D_kx\to x^*Dx$ and $x^*(I_n-D_k)x\to x^*(I_n-D)x$. Since both sequences are nonnegative, their limits are nonnegative, so $0\preceq D\preceq I_n$. Finite sums commute with coordinate limits, hence $\operatorname{tr}D=\lim_k\operatorname{tr}D_k=r$. Therefore $D\in\mathcal D_r$.

The finitely many entries converge, so the sum of their squared absolute errors tends to zero; thus $\|D_k-D\|_F\to0$. Every Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ therefore converges there, proving completeness. Any ambient-convergent sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ is Cauchy, so the same limit argument shows its limit belongs to $\mathcal D_r$; this proves closedness.

If $D_1,D_2\in\mathcal D_r$ and $t\in[0,1]$, then $tD_1+(1-t)D_2$ is Hermitian; its quadratic form and that of $I_n-tD_1-(1-t)D_2$ are convex combinations of nonnegative quadratic forms, and its trace is $t\operatorname{tr}D_1+(1-t)\operatorname{tr}D_2=tr+(1-t)r=r$. Hence it lies in $\mathcal D_r$, proving convexity.

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

$$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$

If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then

$$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a
real-linear map $L$ such that

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0).$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted
$DF(A)$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

derivations.claim: By [F1], there is a unique $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. In the projector application, [L1] supplies the stated map wherever the strict gap hypothesis holds.

Then both $\operatorname{ran}P$ and $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ are invariant under $F$: if $x=Px$, then $P(Fx)=F(Px)=Fx$, and the analogous identity holds when $Px=0$. Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and

$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Input: a complete invariant set $K$ and a gapped response map $\Phi:K\to K$

1. If no certified response evaluation is cached for $P_k$, evaluate the finite-basis matrix $F(P_k)$ and its occupied projector solver. If the gap fails, return $\texttt{gap-loss}$; if the eigensolver cannot certify its output/error, return $\texttt{eigensolve-failure}$. [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

If $D\in\mathcal D_r$ and the gapped map $\Phi(D)$ of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] is defined, then for every
$\alpha\in[0,1]$,
$$D^+=(1-\alpha)D+\alpha\Phi(D)$$
belongs to $\mathcal D_r$. The conclusion does not assert $D^+\in\mathcal P_r$.

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A

exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical

Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

Input: current $P_k\in\mathcal P_r$, up to $m-1$ earlier stored projectors
$P_i$ and their Hermitian matrices $F(P_i)$, memory cap $m\ge1$, coefficient
cap $C\ge1$, and an exact or certified solver for the constrained least-squares
problem. The procedure is one proposal step:

1. Form each commutator residual $R_i=[F(P_i),P_i]:=F(P_i)P_i-P_iF(P_i)$ for the stored history together with the current iterate. Retain at most the most recent $m$ residuals.
2. Find coefficients minimizing $\|\sum_i c_iR_i\|_F^2$ subject to $\sum_i c_i=1$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. If the configured linear-system solver reports a singular system or cannot certify a minimizer, return $(P_k,\texttt{singular-or-uncertified-ls})$ and request the baseline SCF update. If it returns multiple minimizers, select the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm minimizer supplied by [[lem-capped-diis-coefficient-minimizer-exists]].
3. If the returned coefficients fail either constraint, return $(P_k,\texttt{coefficient-cap-failure})$ and request the baseline update. Otherwise form $F_{mix}=\sum_i c_iF(P_i)$. If the $r$th gap of $F_{mix}$ is not certified, return $(P_k,\texttt{candidate-gap-failure})$ and request the baseline update.
4. Return the projector $Y=\Pi_r(F_{mix})$ as a DIIS candidate.

The commutator least-squares objective defines a proposal; it is not a fixed-point
error certificate. The outer safeguarded procedure checks $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$
separately before accepting a candidate. This algorithm makes no bare DIIS
convergence claim.

each required iterate, a fixed mixing parameter $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a fixed-point
residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, and a finite update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,N$, first certify that the occupied gap at
$D_k$ is positive. If the eigensolver fails, return
$(D_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},\varnothing,k)$; if the gap is absent, return
$(D_k,\texttt{gap-loss},\varnothing,k)$. Otherwise evaluate $\Phi(D_k)$ and
$$r_k=\|D_k-((1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k))\|_F.$$
If $r_k\le\varepsilon$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{residual-tolerance-met},r_k,k)$. If $k=N$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},r_k,k)$. Otherwise update
$$D_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k)$$
and continue.

update stays in $\mathcal D_r$; it need not be idempotent. This algorithm is the

map. It makes no convergence claim unless the derivative-bound and invariance
hypotheses in [[thm-density-mixing-contracts-under-jacobian-certificate]] are
verified. If $\alpha=0$, then the relaxed residual is identically zero and the
update does not move; that stop status alone says nothing about the unmixed
response residual.
